citeAs: Paperno, D., Kruszewski, G., Lazaridou, A., Pham, Q. N., Bernardi, R., Pezzelle, S., Baroni, M., Boleda, G., & Fernández, R. (2016). The LAMBADA dataset: Word prediction requiring a broad discourse context. arXiv:1606.06031.
creator: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández (CIMeC - Center for Mind/Brain Sciences, University of Trento; Institute for Logic, Language & Computation, University of Amsterdam)
description: LAMBADA (LAnguage Modeling Broadened to Account for Discourse Aspects) is a collection of narrative passages where human subjects can guess the last word when exposed to the whole passage, but not when only seeing the last sentence. It evaluates computational models' ability to use broad discourse context for word prediction, consisting of 10,022 passages divided into development and test sets sourced from the BookCorpus.
name: LAMBADA
publisher: CIMeC - Center for Mind/Brain Sciences, University of Trento
rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 2 full-passage annotations (steps 1 and 2), plus up to 10 sentence-only annotation attempts (step 3, with 3 guesses each).
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: In the crowdsourcing pipeline, 84–86% of items were discarded at step 1, an additional 6–7% at step 2, and another 3–5% at step 3. Only about one in 25 input examples passed all selection steps. The dataset required exact word match for inclusion.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Three-step crowdsourcing pipeline: (1) one subject guessed the target word from the full passage; if correct, (2) a second subject guessed from the full passage; if also correct, (3) up to 10 subjects tried to guess from the target sentence only (with 3 guesses each). A passage was included in LAMBADA only if steps 1 and 2 succeeded and step 3 produced no correct guess. Subjects were paid $0.22 per page in steps 1 and 2 (10 passages/page) and $0.15 per page in step 3 (20 sentences/page).
rai:dataBiases: Target words are heavily skewed toward proper nouns (48%) and common nouns (37%), with verbs, adjectives, and adverbs underrepresented compared to general text. More than 80% of LAMBADA passages include the target word in the context. The dataset contains quoted direct speech significantly more often than the input items (71% vs. 61%). The filtering process by design excludes passages guessable by standard language models.
rai:dataCollection: Passages were sourced from the BookCorpus (unpublished novels). Candidate passages were filtered by automated language models to remove easy-to-guess items, then evaluated by human subjects via CrowdFlower crowdsourcing in a three-step pipeline: two subjects independently guessed the target word from the full passage, and then up to 10 subjects tried to guess from the last sentence only. Only passages where both full-context guesses were correct and no sentence-only guess succeeded were included.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw source data is the BookCorpus, containing 5,325 novels and 465 million words after duplicate removal and filtering of potentially offensive material. The corpus contains unpublished novels.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataLimitations: LAMBADA was designed to challenge language models with harder-than-average examples; standard language models are bound to fail on it by design since one of the first filters was to choose passages where simple language models failed. The dataset is limited to English narrative text from unpublished novels. The strict hit-or-miss approach for inclusion may exclude valid passages with synonymous correct answers.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The BookCorpus was preprocessed by removing duplicates and filtering out potentially offensive material using a stop word list. Novels were randomly divided into equally-sized training and development+testing partitions. Passages were filtered using a combination of four language models (a pre-trained RNN and three models trained on BookCorpus: a 4-gram model, an RNN, and a feed-forward model); any passage whose target word had probability above 0.00175 according to any model was excluded.
rai:dataSocialImpact: LAMBADA is intended to promote research into language models with genuine broad-context understanding, moving beyond systems that produce locally coherent but globally incoherent language. The authors plan to announce a public competition based on the LAMBADA data to stimulate the community.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating computational models' ability to understand broad discourse context in natural language text, specifically via word prediction. Intended as a challenging benchmark to encourage development of language models capable of genuine understanding of broad context.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Four language models used for automated filtering: a pre-trained RNN (Mikolov et al., 2011), a standard 4-gram language model, an RNN trained on BookCorpus, and a feed-forward language model trained on BookCorpus.

evidence.name: We introduce LAMBADA, a dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task.
evidence.description: LAMBADA is a collection of narrative passages sharing the characteristic that human subjects are able to guess their last word if they are exposed to the whole passage, but not if they only see the last sentence preceding the target word.
evidence.url: The development set of LAMBADA, along with the training corpus, can be downloaded at http://clic.cimec.unitn.it/lambada/

evidence.inLanguage: LAMBADA proposes a word prediction task where the target item is difficult to guess (for English speakers) when only the sentence in which it appears is available
evidence.citeAs: We introduce LAMBADA, a dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task. arXiv:1606.06031v1  [cs.CL]  20 Jun 2016
evidence.isLiveDataset: The LAMBADA dataset consists of 10,022 passages, divided into 4,869 development and 5,153 test passages (extracted from 1,331 and 1,332 disjoint novels, respectively).
evidence.rai:dataCollection: The LAMBADA data come from the Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015). A random sample of the remaining passages were then evaluated by human subjects through the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service in three steps.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: The LAMBADA data come from the Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015). The fact that it contains unpublished novels minimizes the potential usefulness of general world knowledge and external resources for the task.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The corpus, after duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list, contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The corpus, after duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list, contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words. We used a combination of four language models, chosen by availability and/or ease of training: a pre-trained recurrent neural network (RNN) (Mikolov et al., 2011) and three models trained on the Book Corpus (a standard 4-gram model, a RNN and a feed-forward model). Any passage whose target word had probability 0.00175 according to any of the language models was excluded.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: A random sample of the remaining passages were then evaluated by human subjects through the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: one human subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage (comprising the context and the target sentence); if the guess was right, a second subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage; if that guess was also right, more subjects tried to guess the target word based on the target sentence only, until the word was guessed or the number of unsuccessful guesses reached 10; if no subject was able to guess the target word, the passage was added to the LAMBADA dataset.
evidence.rai:annotationsPerItem: more subjects tried to guess the target word based on the target sentence only, until the word was guessed or the number of unsuccessful guesses reached 10; if no subject was able to guess the target word, the passage was added to the LAMBADA dataset. The subjects in step 3 were allowed 3 guesses per sentence.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: In the crowdsourcing pipeline, 84–86% items were discarded at step 1, an additional 6–7% at step 2 and another 3–5% at step 3. Only about one in 25 input examples passed all the selection steps.
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: We used a combination of four language models, chosen by availability and/or ease of training: a pre-trained recurrent neural network (RNN) (Mikolov et al., 2011) and three models trained on the Book Corpus (a standard 4-gram model, a RNN and a feed-forward model; see SM for details)
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: We thus propose LAMBADA as a challenging test set, meant to encourage the development of new models capable of genuine understanding of broad context in natural language text.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: Figure 2(b) shows that most target words in LAMBADA are proper nouns (48%), followed by common nouns (37%) and, at a distance, verbs (7.7%). In fact, proper nouns are hugely over-represented in LAMBADA, while the other categories are under-represented, compared to the POS distribution in the input.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: We also note that, because of the way we have constructed LAMBADA, standard language models are bound to fail on it by design: one of our first filters (see Section 3.1) was to choose passages where a number of simple language models were failing to predict the upcoming word.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: We hope the computational community will be stimulated to develop novel language models that are genuinely capturing the non-local phenomena that LAMBADA reflects. To promote research in this direction, we plan to announce a public competition based on the LAMBADA data.
evidence.datePublished: LAMBADA casts language understanding in the classic word prediction framework of language modeling. We can thus use it to test several existing language modeling architectures, includingarXiv:1606.06031v1 [cs.CL] 20 Jun 2016 systems with capacity to hold longer-term contextual memories.
